rationale: One sentence added to the TimeoutNow account, resting only on receipts already cited there: this run now holds two independent routes to the same consequence, the transfer trigger measured here (e1ee764584564a95b3e288381dfb75d9 at 17 and 18, and 21d5c70cd8a9439594340e00f2d09c11 at 34) and the term adoption of a node left with an empty configuration by a RestoreCommittedLogs restart (e52401f293244c72ae4e1dcb5f6889dd at 38). That matters for the discriminator, which asks what bounds the disruption: closing one route does not close the other, because the second needs no transfer request at all and only a sender that reaches one node with a higher term. No conclusion, counterevidence, citation or evidence is changed; the added sentence is derived from the receipts already listed.

interpretations.joint_history: Two receipts answer this question: the earlier run (e1ee764584564a95b3e288381dfb75d9 at indices 17 and 18) measured one displacement from a removed sender, and this run (21d5c70cd8a9439594340e00f2d09c11 at index 34) repeats the trigger three times from the same sender, so the single displacement and the repetition come from the same scenario shape in the same harness file. A related but distinct route is recorded in receipt e52401f293244c72ae4e1dcb5f6889dd at index 38: a sender that appears in no configuration raised a RestoreCommittedLogs-restarted node's term through one higher-term AppendEntries and the serving leader of a healthy three-voter cluster stepped down, which shares the consequence but not the TimeoutNow mechanism measured here.
interpretations.rationale: Current account: the transfer trigger is not restricted to the current leader, and the same non-member can use it repeatedly. Evidence: the earlier receipt shows one displacement with the serving leader stepping down and the target becoming leader; the later receipt shows three consecutive rounds, each changing leadership, with the term advancing 3, 4, 5 and a leader present after every round. Mechanism from source: timeoutNow clears the known leader, sets the recipient's state to Candidate and stores candidateFromLeadershipTransfer without inspecting the request's RPCHeader, so any transport-reachable peer can trigger the exchange as often as it can reach a voter; the campaign then sets LeadershipTransfer on its vote requests, and requestVote skips its leader-availability rejection when that flag is set, so voters that know a healthy leader still grant. Consequence: a removed or otherwise non-member server that remains transport-reachable can keep displacing the leader, one term per attempt, while the cluster still elects a replacement between attempts, so the effect is persistent disruption of authority rather than a stall or a loss of committed data. The measurement also corrects the account's earlier limitation, which said recurrence had not been measured. Related witness, kept distinct: receipt e52401f293244c72ae4e1dcb5f6889dd at index 38 records a sender that appears in no configuration reaching a node restarted with an empty configuration, adopting the sender's higher term and the node reporting it as leader, after which the serving leader of the healthy cluster stepped down. That is the same class of consequence as this question's, achieved without TimeoutNow, so it is cited as a related witness with its own mechanism named rather than as evidence for the transfer path. Two independent routes to the same consequence are now witnessed in this run, which the next bound has to account for: the transfer trigger measured here, and the term adoption of a node left with an empty configuration by a RestoreCommittedLogs restart (receipt e52401f293244c72ae4e1dcb5f6889dd at index 38), where no transfer request is involved and the sending server need only reach that one node with a higher term.
counterevidence: The cluster reaches a leader between attempts, so each round costs one election and one term bump rather than leaving the cluster without leadership.

Any cluster member can force term changes by campaigning; what makes this path distinct is that it bypasses the voters' leader-availability protection, and that the sender need not be in the configuration at all.

The requests were sent from the removed node's own in-memory transport in a cluster that keeps it reachable, which is the situation of a server taken out of the configuration but not shut down; a deployment that retires the server entirely would not reach it.
No write path is affected: entries, logs and commitment remain consistent, and the disruption is confined to authority and term churn.
limitations: Measured on one three-voter in-memory cluster with shortened timers and three rounds; longer repetition and larger clusters are not covered.
The probe chose each round's target as a surviving follower that was not the current leader, so the measurement covers that selection strategy rather than every possible target choice.

An earlier version of the probe was invalid because the request was delivered back to the sender; that wiring was fixed before the queued run, and the earlier invalid result (no leadership change) is superseded and not used as evidence.
The related witness comes from a different mechanism and a different precondition, an empty recovered configuration rather than a removed member, so it does not extend the transfer path's reach.
